title: Liturgy (CCC 1066–1070)
hookLine: liturgy means the work of the people, now the work of God among us

cards: Stand at the back of a Catholic church during Mass and just listen. The priest says a line, and the whole room answers. He prays, and the room says amen.

People stand, sit, kneel, sing, walk forward, go quiet, all together, with hardly anyone giving directions out loud. To a visitor it can look like a show with an audience that happens to know the script.
The Catechism paints a picture with no audience in it at all. Its first part was about what Catholics believe. Its second part is about how they celebrate it, and it opens with one word.

teach.b: The word is liturgy. Back on day seven hundred ninety-one, this path met the Council's call to take part; now, the word underneath. First, where it comes from.
The word originally meant a public work, the Catechism explains, a service done in the name of the people, or on their behalf. Not a private hobby. Second, what the Church did with it.
In Christian use, liturgy means the people of God taking part in the work of God.
And that work is big: through the liturgy, Catholics believe, Christ himself keeps carrying on the work of saving the world, in his Church, with his Church, and through his Church.

teach.h: THE PEOPLE IN THE WORK OF GOD.
teach.b: The people's work and God's work end up being the same work, done together. Third, it's wider than one room. The New Testament uses this word for Zechariah serving in the Temple, in Luke's Gospel.
For preaching the Gospel. And for practical help, like the care one church sent to Paul through a messenger.
Worship, preaching, charity: all of it, liturgy. Fourth, the people have a part. The Second Vatican Council asked for the faithful to take part fully, consciously and actively.
That's one reason the room answers. When the priest says the Lord be with you, the reply isn't politeness. It's the people doing their part of the work.
So there's no audience at Mass. Everyone in the room has a job.

how: At Mass Catholics take part through spoken responses, singing, standing, sitting and kneeling together, and in roles such as reader, server, cantor and minister of Communion.

games.q: you're at Mass for the first time. the priest says, the Lord be with you. what is the room doing?
o: answering, because the people have a part in the work
waiting for the music to start
games.why: the room answers him. the Catechism calls liturgy the people of God taking part in the work of God: there's no audience.

practice: Bring to mind the next shared moment you'll be part of: a Mass, a service, a family meal, a birthday song. Pick one way you'll take part fully instead of watching: answer out loud, sing instead of mouthing, put the phone away.
If you pray, offer it ahead of time; if you don't, simply plan to show up all the way.

wordCard.voice: Liturgy. Once a public work done for the people. For Catholics, the people of God taking part in the work of God, with no one in the room just watching. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: a public work or service. The Catechism says it came to mean the people's share in the work of God.

carryVoice: Your line: the people's work. No one in the room is just watching. Until tomorrow.
